content: The alimentary mucosa was implicated in the reactivation of a duodenal ulcer in this patient. However, no authoritative sources or clinical or experimental evidence were provided to substantiate this claim. Beyond Cherkes' statement that stasis and venous hyperemia occur in the gastrointestinal tract as a result of pulmonary edema, no other references regarding the effects of phosgene on gastrointestinal mucosa were identified. Seidelin documented a case involving a 16-year-old female who likely inhaled phosgene, leading to pulmonary edema. This incident occurred after she used a carbon tetrachloride fire extinguisher in an enclosed space. In 1946, Galdston and colleagues reported on six cases of acute phosgene exposure, with residual effects persisting up to 19 months post-exposure. Their evaluations included physical examinations, chest X-rays, pulmonary function tests, and psychiatric assessments. These cases shared a common history of brief, single exposures to phosgene at unknown concentrations, typically resulting in delayed pulmonary edema. One notable case involved exposure to an ampule containing only 40 mL of phosgene under a hood. All patients were treated at Johns Hopkins Hospital and subsequently discharged, with some resuming normal work routines. However, follow-up examinations revealed persistent complaints. While physical exams and chest X-rays up to 19 months later were generally normal, pulmonary function tests consistently showed abnormalities indicative of early pulmonary emphysema. The authors suggested that psychological factors contributed to the lingering symptoms. Cherkes, in a comprehensive review of the clinical course of acute phosgene exposure, noted that most fatalities occurred within the first 24–48 hours. He reported that patients who died within the first 72 hours typically succumbed to pulmonary edema or cardiac complications, while those who died later often did so due to secondary complications such as infections (usually pulmonary), thrombosis, or embolism. However, Cherkes did not provide specific sources for these statements, citing only the data of various authors. His description of the clinical course following phosgene exposure aligns with other reports from both human and animal studies. Ardran observed that many victims of phosgene poisoning exhibited radiological evidence of increased lung volumes. His experiments with dogs demonstrated that animals failing to develop increased lung volumes after phosgene exposure also failed to develop pulmonary edema. Clinically, he used this observation to predict pulmonary edema. He reported that if an expiratory lung film showed increased volume after phosgene exposure, pulmonary edema was likely to follow. Over 20 years, he never observed pulmonary edema in humans exposed to lung irritants without a preceding increase in lung volume. Arterial blood oxygen, alveolar air oxygen, and carbon dioxide tension studies were conducted at rest and after exercise 4–8 months after all other evaluations were completed. Symptoms, physical findings, and radiographic results remained unchanged upon reexamination of all available patients (except one) at that time. Levina et al. described the working environment in the monuron (3-(p-chlorophenyl)-1,1-dimethylurea) industry, where phosgene exposure was measured at 0 mg/m³ (0.25–0.05 ppm) over a six-month period. Other contaminants included chlorobenzene, dimethylamine, and parachlorophenyl isocyanate. They reported no pulmonary problems among workers but did not explicitly search for them. Levina and Kurando studied a plant manufacturing a weed killer (isopropylphenylcarbamate) using phosgene, isopropyl alcohol, aniline, and caustic soda as raw materials. Among 89 workers studied for hematological abnormalities, methemoglobinemia and anemia were detected, attributed to the weed killer and aniline. No mention was made of pulmonary issues. At a plant manufacturing phosgene, medical records of 326 exposed workers were compared with those of 6,288 non-exposed workers. Pulmonary function, lung problems, and lung-related deaths were analyzed for both groups. The data suggested no chronic lung problems associated with working in phosgene operations. By comparing the age distribution of employees and pensioners and their lung-related deaths with those expected in a similar age group not exposed to phosgene, no increase in lung-related deaths was noted among phosgene-industry workers. The authors attributed differences in the major site of action to the respiratory bronchioles in one case and the alveoli in another. They noted that above a Ct (concentration × time) of 30 ppm-minutes, gas exchange capacity decreased logarithmically with increasing Ct. Rinehart and Hatch observed no significant effects of phosgene on test animals' pulmonary performance at exposures below a Ct of 30 ppm-minutes. Their experiments covered a Ct range of 12–360 ppm-minutes and found that chronic pneumonitis could be induced, which was reversible but left detectable lesions for up to three months. They explained that low doses of phosgene irritated the pulmonary alveolar epithelium, leading to proliferation, while severe exposures destroyed the surface epithelium and attacked the underlying alveolar capillaries, resulting in pulmonary edema. The severity of chronic pneumonitis correlated well with the Ct value of phosgene exposure and appeared largely independent of gas concentration within the same Ct range. Gross et al. exposed animals to Ct products ranging from 13 to 360 ppm-minutes. Among 18 rats exposed to phosgene with Ct products ≤30 ppm-minutes, 28% showed no abnormalities, 61% exhibited slight chronic pneumonitis, and 11% displayed moderate chronic pneumonitis. Wirth studied the effects of low concentrations of phosgene on cats. He reported that the lethal concentration × survival time in minutes was approximately 1,000 when expressed as mg/m³. At low concentrations (5–7 mg/m³, 1–2 ppm), the constant was as high as 3,000, indicating that the lethal Ct product is significantly higher at low concentrations. Wirth attributed this to detoxification and concluded that the practical usefulness of the Ct formula remained valid within certain concentration limits.
